metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD-provided PISA 2000, 2009, and 2015 microdata and estimates multilevel models with student-level and school-level predictors. To compensate for missing observations, the authors apply student weights provided by the OECD, and they explicitly state that these weights are used to correct standard errors and variance decomposition in multilevel models. The analysis also uses a multiple imputation framework for missing data on the dependent variable and on independent variables at both student and school levels, and then reports combined R2 values across imputed datasets. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight uncertainty estimation cannot be extracted from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses official OECD PISA 2000, 2009, and 2015 datasets. For the UK, Scotland is excluded in all three years because it was recorded separately in 2009; Wales is excluded in 2000 because no values were obtained for Welsh students in that wave. The dependent variable is the imputed PISA mean score (reading, mathematics, and science), and the authors apply multiple imputation for missing data on both the dependent variable and independent variables at student and school levels.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 (UK without Scotland; Germany) — imputed mean score (reading, mathematics, science)
main_findings.target_variable: PISA mean score (imputed across reading, mathematics, science)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (student + school levels). Germany: ICC=0.630 (p<0.001); R2 full model=0.480 (p<0.001). UK: ICC=0.288 (p<0.001); R2 full model=0.315 (p<0.001). Key coefficients (full model): Germany student ESCS β=10.343 (p<0.001); Germany school mean ESCS β=105.524 (p<0.001). UK student ESCS β=27.763 (p<0.001); UK school mean ESCS β=62.924 (p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 data (UK without Scotland; Germany) with the imputed mean score across reading, mathematics, and science as the dependent variable, the study leveraged socioeconomic status at both student and school levels (ESCS and school mean ESCS) plus language-at-home and disciplinary climate to explain between-student and between-school variation, finding that school-level socioeconomic inequality was a much stronger predictor than student-level ESCS in both countries. This indicates that education equity efforts targeting school segregation and the socioeconomic composition of schools may be more consequential for performance than governance reforms alone, though the study is correlational and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 (UK without Scotland; Germany) — imputed mean score (reading, mathematics, science)
main_findings.target_variable: PISA mean score (imputed across reading, mathematics, science)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (student + school levels). Germany: ICC=0.577 (p<0.001); R2 full model=0.475 (p<0.001). UK: ICC=0.275 (p<0.001); R2 full model=0.333 (p<0.001). Key coefficients (full model): Germany student ESCS β=10.230 (p<0.001); Germany school mean ESCS β=116.308 (p<0.001). UK student ESCS β=26.365 (p<0.001); UK school mean ESCS β=73.350 (p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 data (UK without Scotland; Germany) with the imputed mean score across reading, mathematics, and science as the dependent variable, the study leveraged student ESCS, school mean ESCS, and language-at-home (plus disciplinary climate) to explain performance differences, finding that school-level socioeconomic inequality remained the dominant predictor while governance variables contributed little to explained variance. This indicates that policies aimed at reducing socioeconomic segregation between schools may be the most effective lever for improving equity in achievement, while school governance reforms should be scrutinized for limited impact on learning outcomes.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (UK without Scotland; Germany) — imputed mean score (reading, mathematics, science)
main_findings.target_variable: PISA mean score (imputed across reading, mathematics, science)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (student + school levels). Germany: ICC=0.528 (p<0.001); R2 full model=0.428 (p<0.001). UK: ICC=0.252 (p<0.001); R2 full model=0.312 (p<0.001). Key coefficients (full model): Germany student ESCS β=10.589 (p<0.001); Germany school mean ESCS β=88.976 (p<0.001). UK student ESCS β=20.989 (p<0.001); UK school mean ESCS β=64.553 (p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 data (UK without Scotland; Germany) with the imputed mean score across reading, mathematics, and science as the dependent variable, the study leveraged student and school socioeconomic status alongside language-at-home and disciplinary climate, finding that socioeconomic inequality at the school level continued to explain a large share of variance and that governance-related indices did not meaningfully offset socioeconomic effects. This indicates that strengthening equity through addressing school composition and segregation is likely to matter more for achievement than expanding autonomy/leadership/accountability reforms, while causality cannot be inferred from the observational multilevel models.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2000, 2009, and 2015 microdata for the UK (excluding Scotland in all waves; excluding Wales in 2000) and Germany, using the imputed PISA mean score across reading, mathematics, and science as the dependent variable. It estimates multilevel regression models with student- and school-level predictors, applying multiple imputation for missing data and OECD-provided student weights to correct standard errors and variance decomposition. Across all three waves, socioeconomic status is consistently associated with performance, but school-level socioeconomic inequality (school mean ESCS) is substantially stronger than student-level ESCS, with large model fit (e.g., Germany R2 full model ≈0.48 in 2000; UK ≈0.315 in 2000) and significant ICCs indicating between-school homogeneity. Governance variables (autonomy, leadership, accountability) show little explanatory power and do not remove socioeconomic associations. Limitations include the correlational design and potential bias from differential PISA participation coverage in the UK versus Germany, which the authors discuss as possibly affecting achievement-gap estimates.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses multilevel regression and multiple imputation, it does not train or evaluate any machine learning predictive models (no ML algorithms are reported). Consequently, the ML technique fields are left empty, and the extraction focuses on the statistical modeling results rather than ML performance. The absence of ML also explains why no PV-specific ML pipeline metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) are available.
